title: Where Skin Keeps Its Water
endLine: Skin seals in water mainly with lipid between dead cells.

scenes.tts: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates, and the air sets how much can. That sweat is water the body chose to spend. Why doesn't the rest seep out through the skin? The outer surface is made of dead cells. So what holds the water in?
scenes.narration: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates, and the air sets how much can. That sweat is water the body chose to spend. Why doesn't the rest seep out through the skin? The outer surface is made of dead cells. So what holds the water in?

scenes.visual: Open on the first film's picture, same colours: the GREY bar labelled 'skin' near the bottom of the frame, one BLUE drop on it evaporating as wavy BLUE vapour lines rising into the air, one GREY drop beside it dripping off. Colour map, carried from the first film where it continues: GREY = skin and structure, dead cells; BLUE = water (sweat, and water held in the body); new in this film: GOLD = lipid between cells, TEAL = tracer, PURPLE = tight junctions (dry exchange, PURPLE in the first film, does not appear here); living cells are drawn pale peach with a dark nucleus dot. On 'the rest', many small BLUE dots appear below the skin bar, drifting slowly, held in. On 'seep out', a few BLUE dots nudge up against the skin bar and stop. On 'dead cells', the camera pushes into the skin bar, which opens into the film's one world, kept to the end: a schematic cross-section of thin skin filling about 70% of the frame height. From top: air; 3 or 4 rows of flat GREY plates; 3 rows of pale peach living cells with nuclei; a wavy base line; a dark tan dermis band at the bottom with BLUE dots in it. A BLUE sweat duct coils up from the dermis through the epidermis to a pore at the surface. Tag 'schematic' at bottom right throughout. Large white question across the top: 'What holds the water in?'

Title 'Where Skin Keeps Its Water' fades in above the skin section for 2 s while the question text fades. BLUE dots drift slowly in the dermis and living layers; the GREY plates at the top shimmer faintly.

scenes.tts: The outer layer, the epidermis, has no blood vessels. Its cells divide at the base and move outward, like a conveyor belt. On the way they fill with keratin and die. They end as corneocytes: flat cells packed with keratin, with no nucleus.
scenes.narration: The outer layer, the epidermis, has no blood vessels. Its cells divide at the base and move outward, like a conveyor belt. On the way they fill with keratin and die. They end as corneocytes: flat cells packed with keratin, with no nucleus.
scenes.caption: The outer layer, the epidermis, has no blood vessels. Its cells divide at the base and move outward, like a conveyor belt. On the way they fill with keratin and die. They end as corneocytes: flat cells packed with keratin, with no nucleus.
scenes.visual: Same section. Label 'epidermis' brackets the plates and living rows; label 'dermis' sits on the tan band. On 'divide at the base', one peach cell in the bottom row splits in two. On 'move outward', the daughter cell rides slowly upward row by row (the conveyor). On 'fill with keratin', it fills with GREY streaks and flattens. On 'die', its nucleus dot fades out and it becomes a flat GREY plate joining the top rows. Layer labels appear on the right, one per row group, 5 words or fewer: 'basale', 'spinosum', 'granulosum', 'corneum'; small tag 'thin skin' under them. On 'corneocytes', the top GREY plates pulse with label 'corneocytes: dead, no nucleus'. The conveyor keeps running slowly in the background for the rest of the film.

scenes.tts: This wall keeps most water in, so the body can spend water on purpose. A small, steady leak crosses all the time. Large losses go through sweat ducts, when the brain calls for them.
scenes.narration: This wall keeps most water in, so the body can spend water on purpose. A small, steady leak crosses all the time. Large losses go through sweat ducts, when the brain calls for them.
scenes.caption: This wall keeps most water in, so the body can spend water on purpose. A small, steady leak crosses all the time. Large losses go through sweat ducts, when the brain calls for them.
scenes.visual: BLUE dots crowd under the GREY plates and stay below them. On 'small, steady leak', a sparse trickle of single BLUE dots crosses the plates and drifts into the air; label 'small, steady leak'. On 'sweat ducts', the BLUE duct brightens and a stream of BLUE drops travels up it to the pore, spreads on the surface and evaporates as BLUE vapour lines, as in the first film; label 'sweat: spent on purpose'. No numbers.

scenes.tts: Where is the seal? Gut and kidney linings seal the spaces between their cells with tight junctions. So the natural guess was that skin does too, between its living cells.
scenes.narration: Where is the seal? Gut and kidney linings seal the spaces between their cells with tight junctions. So the natural guess was that skin does too, between its living cells.
scenes.caption: Where is the seal? Gut and kidney linings seal the spaces between their cells with tight junctions. So the natural guess was that skin does too, between its living cells.
scenes.visual: The spaces between cells highlight as thin dark lanes running up through the living rows to the plates. On 'Gut and kidney linings', a small inset at top left shows a single row of cells with short PURPLE bars closing the gaps between them, labelled 'gut, kidney: tight junctions'. On 'the natural guess', a dashed PURPLE line with a question mark stretches across the living rows of the main section, labelled 'expected seal?'. The inset fades out.

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-five, Peter Elias and Daniel Friend tested that guess in newborn mouse skin. They followed tracers that dissolve in water and look dense under the electron microscope. The tracers travel in the spaces between cells. If tight junctions were the seal, the tracers would stop there.
scenes.narration: In 1975, Peter Elias and Daniel Friend tested that guess in newborn mouse skin. They followed tracers that dissolve in water and look dense under the electron microscope. The tracers travel in the spaces between cells. If tight junctions were the seal, the tracers would stop there.
scenes.caption: In 1975, Peter Elias and Daniel Friend tested that guess in newborn mouse skin. They followed tracers that dissolve in water and look dense under the electron microscope. The tracers travel in the spaces between cells. If tight junctions were the seal, the tracers would stop there.
scenes.visual: Tag at top left: 'newborn mouse skin, 1975'; small label 'electron microscope view (schematic)'. TEAL tracer dots enter the lanes between the bottom living cells and travel upward along them. On 'would stop there', faint ghost TEAL dots pile up at the dashed PURPLE 'expected seal?' line and halt there; ghost label 'prediction if junctions seal'.

scenes.tts: Instead, the tracers slipped past the lower layers. They stopped high in the granular layer. There, lipid-filled granules called lamellar bodies had emptied into the spaces between cells. The authors placed the main barrier in that lipid.
scenes.narration: Instead, the tracers slipped past the lower layers. They stopped high in the granular layer. There, lipid-filled granules called lamellar bodies had emptied into the spaces between cells. The authors placed the main barrier in that lipid.
scenes.caption: Instead, the tracers slipped past the lower layers. They stopped high in the granular layer. There, lipid-filled granules called lamellar bodies had emptied into the spaces between cells. The authors placed the main barrier in that lipid.
scenes.visual: The ghost dots fade. The real TEAL dots pass the dashed PURPLE line, which fades away, and keep rising through the lanes. In the top granulosum row, small GOLD granules inside the cells (label 'lamellar bodies') move to the cell edges and empty, spilling GOLD into the lanes above them and between the GREY plates. On 'stopped high in the granular layer', the TEAL dots reach the GOLD and halt in a line just beneath it, jiggling slightly. Label on the GOLD: 'lipid: main barrier'.

scenes.tts: Later work showed this lipid as patterned layers between corneocytes, often pictured as bricks in mortar. Here is the idea. Skin's main water seal is lipid packed between dead cells, not junctions between living ones.
scenes.narration: Later work showed this lipid as patterned layers between corneocytes, often pictured as bricks in mortar. Here is the idea. Skin's main water seal is lipid packed between dead cells, not junctions between living ones.
scenes.caption: Later work showed this lipid as patterned layers between corneocytes, often pictured as bricks in mortar. Here is the idea. Skin's main water seal is lipid packed between dead cells, not junctions between living ones.
scenes.visual: Camera eases up to the top rows: the GREY plates and the GOLD between them now fill most of the frame. The GOLD resolves into thin stacked stripes between the plates; GREY plates read as bricks, GOLD as mortar; label 'bricks in mortar'. On 'Here is the idea', BLUE dots below press up against the GOLD and turn back. Large white line across the top during the last sentence: 'Main seal: lipid between dead cells'. Camera eases back out to the full section.

scenes.tts: Then tight junctions came back. Mice were bred without claudin one, a tight junction protein. If lipid is the main seal, should losing that protein matter much?
scenes.narration: Then tight junctions came back. Mice were bred without claudin-1, a tight junction protein. If lipid is the main seal, should losing that protein matter much?
scenes.caption: Then tight junctions came back. Mice were bred without claudin-1, a tight junction protein. If lipid is the main seal, should losing that protein matter much?
scenes.visual: Short PURPLE bars appear between neighbouring cells in the granulosum rows only, just below the GOLD, labelled 'tight junctions, granular layer'. A tag slides in at top left: 'mice: no claudin-1'. On 'losing that protein', the PURPLE bars dim to faint outlines. Question card across the top in white: 'Does losing claudin-1 matter?' BLUE dots wait beneath the GOLD.
Predict pause. Hold the question card and the faint PURPLE outlines. BLUE dots drift beneath the GOLD; the conveyor creeps slowly. No other change.

scenes.tts: It mattered a great deal. In two thousand two, Furuse and colleagues found these mice died within a day of birth. They lost too much water through the skin. So tight junctions in the granular layer also contribute.
scenes.narration: It mattered a great deal. In 2002, Furuse and colleagues found these mice died within a day of birth. They lost too much water through the skin. So tight junctions in the granular layer also contribute.
scenes.caption: It mattered a great deal. In 2002, Furuse and colleagues found these mice died within a day of birth. They lost too much water through the skin. So tight junctions in the granular layer also contribute.
scenes.visual: The question card dissolves. With the PURPLE bars still faint, a stream of BLUE dots leaks up through the upper layers and out into the air (schematic route); a small vertical gauge at right labelled 'water lost (schematic)' fills high. Tag 'Furuse and colleagues, 2002' and a label 'died within a day of birth' appear at top left (text only, no animal drawn). On 'also contribute', the PURPLE bars return to full colour, the leak slows back to the small, steady trickle, and the gauge drops.

scenes.tts: So the seal works in layers. Dead cells, mortared with lipid and helped by junctions beneath, hold your water in. The body then spends water where it chooses, through sweat ducts, and the air decides how much can evaporate.
scenes.narration: So the seal works in layers. Dead cells, mortared with lipid and helped by junctions beneath, hold your water in. The body then spends water where it chooses, through sweat ducts, and the air decides how much can evaporate.
scenes.caption: So the seal works in layers. Dead cells, mortared with lipid and helped by junctions beneath, hold your water in. The body then spends water where it chooses, through sweat ducts, and the air decides how much can evaporate.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full section. On 'Dead cells', the GREY plates pulse; on 'mortared with lipid', the GOLD pulses; on 'junctions beneath', the PURPLE bars pulse. BLUE dots stay held below. On 'sweat ducts', BLUE drops rise up the duct, spread on the surface and evaporate as BLUE vapour lines into the air, the first film's picture returning at the top of the frame.

End card over the dimmed but still moving skin section (conveyor creeping, BLUE dots held beneath the GOLD, a slow trickle of BLUE vapour from the pore). Large white text, centred: 'Skin seals in water mainly with lipid between dead cells.'
